images.caption: In 1879, the Tempelhof repair shop was built on the southern site, followed ten years later by the Tempelhof marshalling yard. From 1923 to 1931, it was expanded into a high-performance marshalling yard for the Halle/Leipzig-Berlin and Dresden-Berlin rail lines. The 50-meter-high water tower was built there in 1927, and the Priesterweg station was built in 1928. In 1952, marshalling operations ceased, and the western operational area of ​​Tempelhof was abandoned. With the construction of the Berlin Wall, the site lost all of its importance.
images.alt: In 1879, the Tempelhof repair shop was built on the southern site, followed ten years later by the Tempelhof marshalling yard. images.caption: The Hohenzollerdamm Bridge spans the urban motorway and the railway tracks. Visible on the left are the station building and the entrance to the Hohenzollerndamm S-Bahn station. images.caption: West Berlin’s BVG had resumed operations on the Wannsee Line in February 1985. The railway bridges passing over Albrechtstraße also created a bottleneck for road traffic, as they were too low. They were raised in succession, first the S-Bahn tracks (including the platform) and subsequently the freight tracks. All work was completed by May 1992.

At the platform above, a train from the NI service group is shown arriving from Frohnau, bound for Lichtenrade.

images.caption: The station was located on the Deutsche Reichsbahn (GDR) S-Bahn line NII, running from Lichterfelde Süd to Heiligensee. Half-trains of the Class 275 (ET 165) series operated at 20-minute intervals. The line was closed after the BVG took over S-Bahn operations in West Berlin. It reopened in May 1995 as line S25, with the station now named Eichborndamm.
images.alt: The station was located on the Deutsche Reichsbahn (GDR) S-Bahn line NII, running from Lichterfelde Süd to Heiligensee. It reopened in May 1995 as line S25, with the station now named Eichborndamm.

images.caption: Train group NI (running between Frohnau and Lichtenrade) and train group NII (running between Heiligensee and Lichterfelde Süd) stopped here. The last Deutsche Reichsbahn trains called at Schönholz on January 8, 1984. The following day, the Reichsbahn suspended operations on this line, as the operating rights were henceforth held by the West Berlin BVG.

images.caption:
Get thelarge view!
Der Molecule Man ist ein Berliner Monumentalkunstwerk, welches 1998/1999 von dem amerikanischen Bildhauer Jonathan Borofsky in der Spree nahe der Elsenbrücke und in der Nähe der Bezirksgrenze von Kreuzberg und Treptow-Köpenick aufgebaut wurde. Es handelt sich dabei um drei 30 Meter hohe Männer aus Aluminium, die sich gegenüberstehen und in der Mitte treffen, was das Zusammentreffen der Bezirke Kreuzberg, Treptow und Friedrichshain symbolisieren soll. Das Kunstwerk wiegt etwa 45 Tonnen.
Der Körper der Figuren ist von Löchern durchsetzt, die die Moleküle symbolisieren sollen, aus denen sie bestehen. Nach Aussage des Künstler soll dies daran erinnern,

   „dass sowohl der Mensch als auch die Moleküle in einer Welt der Wahrscheinlichkeit existieren und dass Ziel aller kreativen und geistigen Traditionen ist, Ganzheit und Einheit innerhalb der Welt zu finden.“

Zu sehen ist das Kunstwerk auch von der Oberbaumbrücke. Finanziert wurde das Kunstwerk durch die Allianz AG, die im nahe stehenden Treptowers ihren Sitz hat.
Der Berliner Volksmund hat schnell andere Bezeichnungen für dieses Wahrzeichen gefunden: Die Skulptur wird in Anspielung auf die Löcher Die Dreikäsehoch oder Calgon-Männer genannt.

images.caption: Berlin, Germany: Theater am Kurfürstendamm Berlin-Charlottenburg, Kurfürstendamm 208-209 Originally built 1904-1905. 1908 installation of a theatre hall. 1921-1923 installation of a theatre proper. 1925 rebuilding by Oskar Kaufmann. 1930-1931 major rebuilding by Oskar Kaufmann for the theatre director, Max Reinhardt. 1936 rebuilding by Carl Cramer. Damaged in World War II. After 1945, restoration and auditorium simplification by Helmut Remmelmann and Fritz Gaulke. Subsequently used by the "Freie Volksbühne" company. 1971 exterior rebuilding by Sigrid Kressmann-Zschach, incorporating the theatre hall in the new "Kurfürstendamm-Karree" complex. Used as a private theatre for light drama and comedy performances.
